slides.title: Copilot creates value, but less than claimed
Copilot is worth launching for its productivity gain, but its retention and win-back effects are smaller than assumed

claims.claim: Copilot lifts dispatcher productivity, but the proof so far comes from volunteers
evidence: 11% more jobs per dispatcher-hour in beta accounts, against 2% for matched accounts

claims.claim: Copilot's effect on retention is unproven, and AI explains few of the customers who leave
evidence: 6% of churned accounts left mainly to switch for AI features

claims.claim: Deals lost to Routewise are worth far less than the sales memo assumes
evidence: −7 pp change in win rate against Routewise since Q2 2026, worth at most $0.6M of new ARR a year (1c2)
1c is an upper bound: it assumes all of the win-rate drop is due to Routewise's AI

claims.claim: Launch on the productivity case and price for it; count no retention or win-back gain in the business case

slides.title: 1a: Copilot appears to save dispatchers time: beta users report 4.1 hours a week and schedule 11% more jobs per hour

claims.claim: Beta accounts report saving 4.1 dispatcher hours a week
evidence: 4.1 dispatcher hours saved a week, as reported by beta accounts
Reported by the 240 beta accounts over the 12-week beta

claims.claim: They also scheduled 11% more jobs per dispatcher-hour, against 2% for matched accounts
evidence: Change in jobs per dispatcher-hour: Beta accounts 0.11; Matched non-beta accounts 0.02
Matched accounts were not offered Copilot; each group is compared with its own prior 12 weeks

claims.claim: Self-reported, with no matched comparison
evidence: Not measured from usage logs, so it may overstate the saving
The pack has no dispatcher wage, so the hours are not priced

slides.title: 1a: That gain is proven only among volunteers, whose accounts are larger and more active than the base

claims.claim: Beta accounts are larger than the base
evidence: 8.1 seats per beta account on average
Against 6.2 seats for all accounts
Beta accounts chose to join; they were not picked at random
Larger accounts have more dispatcher time to save
A gain measured on them may not hold for a small contractor

claims.claim: Usage sits with a few heavy accounts
evidence: 58% of all AI requests came from the top 10% of beta accounts
The mean account sends 3,600 requests a month, the median 1,900
The average gain may come mostly from heavy users
Light users may see little change in their week

claims.claim: 2.5% of all accounts were in the beta
evidence: 240 of 9,800 accounts, over 12 weeks
No random holdout within the volunteers
Twelve weeks is short for a lasting productivity effect
A test on non-volunteers is needed before counting the gain at scale

claims.claim: Treat the productivity gain as the reason to launch, and prove it on non-volunteers in a controlled Q1 2027 test

slides.title: 1b: Higher renewal among beta accounts cannot yet be credited to Copilot, because the accounts chose to join

claims.claim: The gap may mix self-selection with any Copilot effect
evidence: 90-day renewal rate: Beta accounts 0.97; Matched non-beta accounts 0.93
Beta accounts: chose to join, and are larger and more active than the base, traits that renew more anyway
Matched accounts: the pack does not say what they were matched on, and no matching covers the choice to volunteer
What is missing: a randomized group that was offered Copilot and a group that was not
the pack gives no confidence interval for either rate

claims.claim: Count no retention gain in the business case until a randomized test shows one

slides.title: 1b: AI is a minor reason customers leave: only 6% of churned accounts switched for AI features

claims.claim: Retention cannot carry the Copilot case
evidence: Main reason for churning, n = 1,190: Mobile app reliability 0.27; Price 0.22; Other 0.16; Missing integrations 0.15; Went out of business / sold 0.14; Switched for AI features 0.06
AI features: the smallest named reason, behind every operational one
Mobile reliability: the top reason, the subject of section 4
Price: the second reason, a warning against a costly add-on

claims.claim: 0.7 pp: Most NRR Copilot could add by stopping every AI-driven loss
evidence: 14% logo churn × 9,800 accounts would give 1,372 and raise the figure by about 15%

slides.title: 1c: Brightwork's win rate against Routewise fell from 44% to 37% as Routewise bundled AI and cut its price

claims.claim: Win rate in deals where Routewise competed fell
Two changes landed together, so the drop cannot be pinned on AI alone
evidence: AI bundle: Routewise put AI scheduling into its Pro plan in September 2026
Price cut: in the same quarter Routewise offered 20% off the first year
Loss notes: 31% of Q3 lost deals mention AI features, but a mention is not the reason for the loss
Exposure: Routewise competes in about 60% of the 2,600 qualified opportunities a year
Q3 losses are not split by reason

slides.title: 1c: Recovering the whole win-rate drop would bring back about 109 deals a year, a third of the memo's claim

claims.claim: New business won back by restoring the win rate against Routewise is at most $0.6M new ARR a year
evidence: 1,560 opportunities a year where Routewise competes (2,600 × 60%) × −7 pp = 109 deals a year lost to the drop
109 × $5,877.6 Core ARR of a new 6.2-seat account = $0.6M new ARR a year at most

claims.claim: This is an upper bound, and the memo's claim is three times it
evidence: All of the drop is credited to Routewise's AI; none to its 20% first-year discount
The memo's 'about a third of the deals we lose to Routewise' is about 328 of 983 losses a year, three times the whole drop
Copilot can only win back deals lost since Routewise's change, unless it beats Routewise's AI
A won deal is a 6.2-seat Core account; Pro would add to it

slides.title: BACKUP: The Pro economics rest on eight inputs from the briefing pack

claims.claim: Eight inputs
evidence: Pro take-up within a year 33%: 2023 higher-tier launch (§6)
Seats per account 6.2: All accounts (§1)
Pro premium per seat per month $12: Tier option (§6)
AI requests per Pro account a month 3,600: Beta mean account (§5, Table 2)
Inference cost per request $0.01: Provider contract, fixed through December 2027 (§5)
Run cost a year $0.6M: Platform, evaluation and support (§5)
Cost per engineer-year $210K: Fully loaded (§9)
Engineers for two quarters 14: Launch requirement (§3)

slides.title: BACKUP: Without an allowance, margin would fall below the floor if Pro accounts used Copilot like add-on buyers

claims.claim: Margin by usage level
evidence: Beta median 1,900: 77.0%, Above
Beta mean (base case) 3,600: 76.0%, Above
Full allowance, 667 per seat × 6.2 seats 4,135: 75.7%, Above
Add-on buyers' level, no allowance 6,800: 74.1%, Below
3,234 Pro accounts at $0.009 per request plus $0.6M run cost; gross profit today $44.93M; ARR with Pro $60.49M

slides.title: BACKUP: Mobile-driven churn costs more Core ARR than any other reason customers give for leaving

claims.claim: Core ARR lost a year by churn reason
evidence: Mobile app reliability 27%, 321, $1.89M
Missing integrations 15%, 178, $1.05M
Went out of business / sold 14%, 167, $0.98M
Switched for AI features 6%, 71, $0.42M
1,190 accounts churned in 2026 (Table 3); $5,878 Core ARR per 6.2-seat account; 14% logo churn × 9,800 would give 1,372 and raise every figure by about 15%

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Launch Copilot in Q2 2027 inside a Pro tier at $12 more per seat, not as a $149 add-on; include 667 AI requests per seat a month; test Pro on non-beta accounts in Q1 2027; restart the mobile rewrite in Q3 2027 and hold the mobile delay to two quarters; manage five measures (Pro take-up at 26% or more, margin at 75% or more).

alternatives_considered.option: Pro tier at $12 more per seat
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended: ahead of the add-on above 28% take-up; matches the market. About $2.9M ARR at 33% take-up; margin about 76.0%; edge over the add-on rests on one precedent.

Rejected: Twice the revenue per account, but 14% is a volunteer best case and buyers are heavy users; at most $2.45M ARR vs. the $8M proposed from survey intent; inference absorbs 41% of its price for the average buyer.
Rejected: No NRR gain; breaks the floor above 56% usage; margin about 73.5% if every account uses it.

alternatives_considered.option: Copilot first (Copilot in Q2 2027; mobile rewrite resumes Q3 2027)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended: fits the 2028 NRR deadline and the Routewise threat better, at the price of slower mobile fixes.

alternatives_considered.option: Mobile first (mobile on plan; Copilot slips to Q4 2027)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Not chosen: loses less ARR for good if the rewrite works and addresses the top churn reason first, but Pro ramp runs to the end of 2028; delaying mobile loses more ARR for good only if the rewrite would keep over 34% of mobile churners.
Left out: Out of scope: headcount is a fixed constraint of the brief.
Left out: No price evidence beyond $12 and $149; the Q1 2027 offer test can try a second price.
Left out: Outside Brightwork's control; fixed through December 2027 and upside only.
Left out: A Core pricing question, outside this decision.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: All figures from the internal briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data)
Productivity gain is self-reported and proven only among volunteers; no random holdout; twelve weeks is short for a lasting productivity effect
Beta renewal gap may mix self-selection with any Copilot effect; the pack gives no confidence interval for either rate; no retention gain counted
Win-back estimate is an upper bound: it assumes all of the win-rate drop is due to Routewise's AI; Q3 losses are not split by reason
Churn figures based on 1,190 churned accounts; 14% logo churn × 9,800 would give 1,372 and raise figures by about 15%
The 14% paywall rate comes from volunteers, so the rate across the base is likely lower; no discounts, and every buyer stays the full year
Pro take-up of 33% rests on one precedent (2023 tier with different content), so 33% is a precedent, not a forecast
Accounts that move have the average 6.2 seats and all Pro revenue counts toward NRR
NRR needed assumes churn and other expansion held at today's level
Usage set at the beta mean of 3,600 requests a month; inference at the contracted $0.009 per request, fixed through December 2027
Upside not counted: list prices fell 35% in the past year
Payback: take-up ramp moves payback to about 27 months; sales and marketing costs of the launch are not in the pack and are left out
Mobile side assumes the rewrite stops all mobile-driven churn the day it ships; any weaker effect shrinks it
The two-quarter mobile delay is affordable only if it does not grow
Ratings in the packaging comparison are team judgment
Highest risk: take-up below 26%; volunteers and the 2023 tier overstate demand
Risk: Routewise deepens its AI or extends its 20% discount
next_steps: Approve the Q2 2027 launch inside a Pro tier at $12 more per seat, and drop the $149 add-on — CEO and executive team — January 2027 planning
Run a randomized test with non-beta accounts: Pro at $12 per seat against the $149 add-on, with a productivity measure — CPO — Q1 2027
Set the per-seat AI allowance and overage terms, and start the inference contract renegotiation — CFO — Q1 2027
Fix the mobile rewrite restart for Q3 2027 and report mobile churn monthly — Head of Engineering and Head of Customer Success — From Q1 2027
Make Pro the default offer in deals where Routewise competes — VP Sales — From Q2 2027 launch
